entities.name: Sextus Appuleius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Appuleius (born c. 60 BCE, Rome; died 7 BCE) emerged as a prominent Roman senator and administrator during the tumultuous transition from Republic to Empire, serving as a loyal and effective instrument of Augustan authority. His career, marked by high provincial commands and sacerdotal office, exemplifies the new elite forged under Augustus, contributing to the establishment of the Pax Romana through stable governance rather than military conquest. As proconsul of Hispania Tarraconensis and later governor of Asia, Appuleius played a crucial role in consolidating Roman control and integrating vast territories into the nascent imperial system, securing his place among the key figures who shaped the early Augustan age.

Appuleius's distinguished career began with his consulship in 29 BCE, a pivotal year following Octavian's victory at Actium and his triple triumph. This early elevation signaled his close ties to the emerging imperial family; he was the son-in-law of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Augustus's most trusted general and heir apparent, and thus related to Augustus himself. His subsequent appointments were equally significant: he served as proconsul of Hispania Tarraconensis from 23 to 22 BCE, where he likely oversaw administrative reforms and maintained order in a crucial mining province. Later, he held the governorship of Asia, one of the wealthiest and most strategically vital provinces, between 12 and 11 BCE, further demonstrating the emperor's confidence in his administrative capabilities. He also held the prestigious religious office of Augur, underscoring his influence within Roman society.
